documents.title: Why museums are rethinking their night openings
documents.text:
Late-evening openings were once a reliable way for museums to attract young visitors who could not come during the day. Cocktails in the sculpture hall, a live band in the atrium and a ticket price that included a drink drew crowds, and several institutions reported that their under-thirty audience had doubled. Yet a number of directors now admit that the events were less successful than the attendance figures suggested.

Surveys carried out by two museums found that most guests spent barely twenty minutes in the galleries, with the rest of the evening given over to the bar. Relatively few returned during the day. Staff also reported that the noise and crowding made it difficult for those who did wish to look at the works, and that spilled drinks had caused damage to floors and, on one occasion, to a loan from another institution.

Some museums have therefore changed course. Instead of a party, they now offer smaller, quieter evenings built around a single exhibition, with a curator speaking for half an hour and the galleries otherwise left open. Numbers are lower, but the proportion of visitors who return is markedly higher. A director in the north described the shift as "trading a crowd for an audience".

Critics note that the new format is more expensive per head, and that it may be affordable only to larger museums with substantial staff.

questions.prompt: What is the main point of the article?
choices: Museums have stopped opening in the evening
Young visitors no longer care for art
Museums are swapping parties for calm evenings
Cocktail events have raised museum profits
questions.explanation: The article describes why party-style openings are being replaced.

questions.prompt: What did the surveys discover about guests?
choices: Most spent little time at the works
Most were over thirty years old
Most returned during the daytime
Most complained about the ticket price
questions.explanation: Most guests spent barely twenty minutes in the galleries.

questions.prompt: What does 'trading a crowd for an audience' suggest?
choices: The museum wants larger crowds again
Audiences prefer music to exhibitions
Curators dislike speaking to crowds
Fewer attend, but more deeply
questions.explanation: Numbers are lower, but the proportion of visitors who return is higher.

questions.prompt: What limitation of the new format is mentioned?
choices: It cannot be used for loans of art
Smaller museums may find it too costly
It requires a live band each night
It drives away the younger visitors
questions.explanation: It is more expensive per head and may be affordable only to larger museums.

documents.title: Concerning the transfer of the Medina account
documents.text:
To: Rosalind Achebe, Regional Director
From: Felix Dunmore, Account Manager
Subject: Transfer of the Medina Textiles account: handover plan

Dear Rosalind,

As discussed on Tuesday, I am sending the proposed plan for transferring the Medina Textiles account to Chloe Barrow when I move to the Singapore office on 1 April. I have tried to arrange matters so that the client notices as little disruption as possible.

Medina has been a customer for nine years and is our third largest, but it has also been the most demanding. Its buyer, Mr. Ibrahim, expects replies within a few hours and becomes impatient when he is passed from one person to another. For that reason, I propose that Chloe and I attend his next two monthly calls together, so that he can become accustomed to her before I leave. I also suggest that I introduce her at the spring trade fair, which he attends every year.

There is one risk I should flag. Medina's contract is up for renewal in September, and Mr. Ibrahim has hinted that he is considering a competitor's offer. Chloe is capable, but she has not yet handled a renewal. I would therefore ask that you join the negotiations in person, and that I remain available by telephone throughout the summer.

I would be glad to go through the plan with you before Friday.

Best wishes,
Felix

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of the email?
choices: To ask for a promotion in Singapore
To outline a client's handover to a colleague
To warn that a client has left the company
To criticize the buyer's behavior
questions.explanation: He proposes a handover plan for the Medina account.

questions.prompt: What does Mr. Dunmore propose to help Mr. Ibrahim adjust?
choices: A cut in the contract price offered
A visit to the Singapore office soon
Weekly reports written by Chloe Barrow
Shared calls and a fair introduction
questions.explanation: Both attend the next two calls, and he introduces her at the trade fair.

questions.prompt: Why does he want the director involved in the renewal?
choices: His successor lacks experience with renewals

The director negotiates all contracts personally
Chloe Barrow will be on holiday in September
questions.explanation: Chloe 'has not yet handled a renewal' and the client is considering a competitor.

questions.prompt: What is suggested about Mr. Ibrahim?
choices: He plans to cancel the account immediately
He dislikes attending trade fairs
He wants one contact who replies fast
He rarely contacts the company
questions.explanation: He expects quick replies and is impatient when passed between people.

documents.title: Notice of a public consultation on the Riverside development
documents.text:
CITY OF BELLMOOR — NOTICE OF PUBLIC CONSULTATION
Proposed redevelopment of the Riverside depot site

The Planning Department invites residents and business owners to comment on a proposal to redevelop the former Riverside bus depot. The applicant, Halcyon Properties, proposes a mixed-use scheme comprising 210 apartments, a supermarket, a small public square and a bicycle hub, with an underground car park of 180 spaces.

The consultation runs from 3 March to 28 March. Documents, including drawings, traffic assessments and a study of the effect on light to neighboring houses, are available at the Planning Office, at the Central Library and on the city's website. Printed copies can be provided on request, though a small charge applies for the traffic assessment, which exceeds four hundred pages.

Comments should be submitted in writing, by post or electronically, and must include the sender's name and address, as anonymous submissions cannot be considered. Comments that concern matters outside the Council's planning powers, such as the effect of the scheme on property values, will be recorded but cannot influence the decision.

Two public meetings will be held, on 11 March at the Riverside Community Hall and on 19 March at the Central Library, both beginning at 7 p.m. The Planning Committee is expected to decide on the application in June.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of the notice?
choices: To announce the approval of a development
To advertise apartments for sale
To report a traffic study's results
To invite views on a proposed scheme
questions.explanation: The Planning Department invites comments on the redevelopment proposal.

questions.prompt: Why might someone pay a charge for documents?
choices: The library keeps no printed copies
The traffic assessment is very long
Drawings must be ordered from Halcyon
The website is closed to residents
questions.explanation: A small charge applies for the traffic assessment, which exceeds four hundred pages.

questions.prompt: What can be inferred about a comment on property values?
choices: It will be rejected immediately
It will be sent to Halcyon Properties
It is noted, but cannot sway the result
It will decide the application
questions.explanation: Such comments 'will be recorded but cannot influence the decision'.

questions.prompt: Which statement is NOT supported by the notice?
choices: Comments may be sent without a name
The scheme includes a public square
Two public meetings are planned
The decision is expected in June
questions.explanation: Anonymous submissions cannot be considered.

documents.title: Clinical Data Manager, Northgate Biomedical
documents.text:
Northgate Biomedical, an independent research organization conducting clinical trials for new treatments in cardiology, seeks a Clinical Data Manager to join its growing operations team. You will be responsible for the quality and integrity of the data generated by our trials, from the design of collection forms to the final database lock.

The post demands rigor, but also diplomacy. You will work closely with doctors at participating hospitals, many of whom regard data entry as an interruption of patient care, and you will need to persuade them that accurate records are essential to the trial's success. You will also liaise with statisticians, who depend on the cleanliness of your work, and with regulators, who may ask to inspect it.

Candidates should hold a degree in life sciences or a related field and have at least four years' experience of clinical trials, ideally with knowledge of the electronic systems used to capture trial data. Candidates with experience of the regulations governing trials in more than one country will be at an advantage. Because the role involves occasional travel to hospitals, a full driving license is desirable.

We offer a competitive salary, generous leave and the chance to contribute to work that matters. To apply, send your CV and a short statement explaining how you would handle a physician who persistently submits late records.

questions.prompt: What is the main challenge of the job?
choices: Keeping data strict and winning doctors over
Designing new treatments for heart disease
Managing a large team of statisticians
Traveling to hospitals in many countries
questions.explanation: The post demands rigor but also diplomacy with doctors.

questions.prompt: Why will the manager need diplomacy with hospital doctors?
choices: They are all employed directly by Northgate
They dislike electronic systems entirely
They see data entry as a patient distraction
They are openly hostile to regulators
questions.explanation: Many regard data entry as an interruption of patient care.

questions.prompt: What does the application statement reveal about the role?
choices: Physicians never submit their records
Late records from doctors recur often
The firm seeks to dismiss careless doctors
Statisticians review each applicant's statement
questions.explanation: Applicants are asked how they would handle a physician who persistently submits late records.

questions.prompt: Which qualification is described as a possible advantage?
choices: A degree in cardiology or nursing
Experience of managing a hospital
A background in applied statistics
Knowledge of rules in several nations
questions.explanation: Experience of regulations in more than one country 'will be at an advantage'.

documents.title: A lighthouse keeper's last winter
documents.text:
When the lighthouse at Cape Merrow was automated in 1998, it ended a tradition of continuous human watch that had lasted since 1847. The last keeper, Anders Holm, who had served there for twenty-two years, describes the final winter as the loneliest and, to his surprise, the most contented of his life.

"People imagine that a keeper's work was about the light," he said, "but the light looked after itself, more or less. What we really did was watch the weather, record it and be ready." Holm kept a daily log of wind, swell and visibility, which has since been used by climate researchers because it covers a stretch of coast with almost no other measurements. One scientist described the log as "a gift from a man who never knew it would be useful".

Automation brought obvious savings, and nobody now argues for returning to manned stations. Yet Holm believes that something was lost. The keepers, he says, were the only people who noticed when a fishing boat did not return, and on three occasions in his career he raised the alarm before anyone else knew a vessel was missing. A machine, however reliable, does not wonder where a boat has gone.

The tower is now a museum, and Holm, aged seventy-one, occasionally leads visitors up its stairs.

choices: The rise of venture investors in software

questions.explanation: It describes Holm's last winter and what automation changed.

questions.explanation: Researchers use it because the coast has almost no other measurements.

questions.explanation: Keepers noticed when a boat did not return; a machine does not wonder.

questions.prompt: What is implied about Holm's view of automation?
choices: He wants every lighthouse manned again
He accepts its gains but sees a loss
He believes it was unnecessary
He regrets leaving the profession
questions.explanation: Nobody argues for return to manned stations, yet he believes something was lost.
